episode_title: Thrive Causemetics: Karissa Bodnar. How a Beauty Business Made Millions for a Mission
question: How did growing up on a farm influence early interest in cosmetic formulation and chemistry?
transcript_excerpt: Karissa started formulating makeup in her parents' kitchen at age 10, learning chemistry through imagination and experimentation. She ground down sunflower seeds to make butter, steamed rose petals for pigment, and discovered that blackberries could stain hands, realizing this pigment could be used in lipstick or blush. Her parents fostered this creativity by providing her with books like the Cosmetic Ingredient Dictionary before the internet era.

podcast_name: How I Built This with Guy Raz
episode_title: Thrive Causemetics: Karissa Bodnar. How a Beauty Business Made Millions for a Mission
question: What opportunities did working at Sephora provide compared to other retail beauty positions?
transcript_excerpt: At Sephora, Karissa was trained on every single brand and received multiple certifications in artistry, skincare, fragrance, and hair care through different levels. She credited Sephora with raising her and providing her real education in beauty, whereas she had applied to all the beauty counters at other retailers and was rejected because she didn't have the skill set they were looking for at the time.

podcast_name: How I Built This with Guy Raz
episode_title: Thrive Causemetics: Karissa Bodnar. How a Beauty Business Made Millions for a Mission
question: What role did Clarisonic and L'Oreal play in shaping a career in product development?
transcript_excerpt: Clarisonic was a sonic cleansing brush created by the same five founders who pioneered Sonicare, based in Factoria, Washington. While Karissa was working at Sephora, Clarisonic was acquired by L'Oreal within her first year there. Carol Hamilton, president of L'Oreal Lux, saw potential in Karissa and took her to Paris to work with chemists and engineers on luxury brand collaborations, creating devices for Yves Saint Laurent and Lancôme.

podcast_name: How I Built This with Guy Raz
episode_title: Thrive Causemetics: Karissa Bodnar. How a Beauty Business Made Millions for a Mission
question: How did a friend's death from cancer inspire a shift toward purpose-driven entrepreneurship?
transcript_excerpt: In 2013, Christy Lamond, a college friend who dedicated her life to philanthropy and taught English to young girls in Tanzania and Chile, died of cancer at age 24. While Karissa was in Paris presenting to the CEO of L'Oreal at their annual Mondial conference, Christy called to say she had cancer, and she passed away nine months later. Christy's blog 'Wake Up and Live' discussed dying successfully, which profoundly influenced Karissa's decision to leave L'Oreal and create a brand with purpose.

podcast_name: How I Built This with Guy Raz
episode_title: Thrive Causemetics: Karissa Bodnar. How a Beauty Business Made Millions for a Mission
question: What specific problem in the beauty industry for cancer patients inspired the creation of Thrive Causemetics?
transcript_excerpt: While volunteering as a makeup artist with Look Good, Feel Better, an organization providing makeup classes to women going through cancer, Karissa discovered that women who had lost their natural lashes had no solution. Traditional mascara wouldn't work without lashes, and fake lashes with toxic glues filled with latex, parabens, and sulfates were irritating to immune-compromised people and wouldn't stay on. She wanted to create a non-toxic solution that would help people like Christy maintain their dignity and sense of self.

podcast_name: How I Built This with Guy Raz
episode_title: Thrive Causemetics: Karissa Bodnar. How a Beauty Business Made Millions for a Mission
question: How did the Tom's Shoes business model influence the founding approach of Thrive Cosmetics?
transcript_excerpt: Karissa woke up in the middle of the night in Los Angeles during an L'Oreal trip in 2013 and thought about how Tom's had built an engine for giving back through its shoe company. She realized the beauty industry had the budget to give back in a more meaningful way, and she decided to apply that one-for-one model to create Thrive Causemetics as a purpose-driven beauty brand.

podcast_name: How I Built This with Guy Raz
episode_title: Thrive Causemetics: Karissa Bodnar. How a Beauty Business Made Millions for a Mission
question: What financial commitment and employment strategy did Karissa use to launch Thrive Causemetics?
transcript_excerpt: Karissa invested approximately $100,000 of her life savings into starting Thrive Cosmetics. She also worked a full-time job in a different category—the nutrition and coffee industry at Bulletproof Coffee Company—to ensure she remained gainfully employed, as her father had always stressed the importance of maintaining employment while building the business.

podcast_name: How I Built This with Guy Raz
episode_title: Thrive Causemetics: Karissa Bodnar. How a Beauty Business Made Millions for a Mission
question: What early sales challenges did Thrive Causemetics face in its first years?
transcript_excerpt: Karissa struggled to get products into retail stores and pitched to major retailers including Sephora, Nordstrom, Ulta, Anthropologie, and QVC, but they did not see the vision. Sales were mainly online and tiny—a good day was $100 in revenue, and there were many days with no sales. She wiped out her entire life savings funding production through her full-time job.
